title: Questioning the Default SPLS Preprocessing Step
text: Here's the question I actually asked. I have a spectroscopy classifier with a baseline correction step called a SPLS sitting in the default pipeline. Nobody has checked whether it earns its place. Predict what happens to test accuracy if I remove it. Tell me where your number comes from, and tell me what would make that number wrong. The answer came back confident, two to five points. It was wrong. Accuracy went up, not down, and it went up by more than the whole predicted range, but that

title: The Initial Prediction vs. Seed Variance Calibration
text: Is not the interesting part. The interesting part is that the number and the reasoning failed in two completely different ways, and only one of them is worth learning from. First, what ASPLS does. Raman spectra arrive sitting on a slow wandering baseline, fluorescence mostly, which carries no information about the molecule you care about. Baseline correction subtracts that drift, so the sharp peaks stand alone. It is standard, it is in the default pipeline, and that is exactly why nobody had questioned it.

title: The Result: A 7.61 Point Gain ($p = 2.5 \times 10^{-57}$)
text: Now, the prediction and where it came from. The estimate was not pulled out of the air, that is what makes it instructive. It was derived from a validation to test pass-through ratio measured on seed variants. In plain terms, run the same model with different random seeds, watch how much test accuracy wobbles, and use that wobble to scale how much a change should move the number. Here is what actually happened. Removing ASPLS did not cost two to five points,

title: The Core Lesson: Randomness Wobble vs. Representation Changes
text: It gained 7.61. The prediction was not just wrong in size, it was wrong in direction. The step that everyone kept because it is standard had been actively hurting the classifier. And before you reach for noise as the explanation, six runs paired McNemar p equals 2.5 * 10 to the -57. That is not a seed that landed well. Paired McNemar is the right test here precisely because the test set is fixed,

title: Re-testing Architecture Assumptions (CNN vs. ResNet)
text: And you are comparing the same samples under two pipelines. So, here is the actual lesson, and it is not be careful, models are sometimes wrong. Seed variance measures one thing, how much the answer moves when you reroll randomness and change nothing else. Removing a pre-processing step is

title: Practical Takeaway: Calibration Questions
text: Not a re-roll. It changes the input representation. The model is now looking at different data. A ratio calibrated on one kind of variation cannot price a different kind. The number being off by 10 points is incidental. The reasoning pattern could not have worked at any magnitude. One more thing because this is the part that keeps you honest. The same reasoning predicted that the repository smaller models win finding was just an artifact of that bad baseline step. 12 runs later at the corrected pipeline, four architectures, three seeds each, legacy CNN still won. 83.89 against ResNet at 79.56. The hypothesis was confidently argued and it was wrong. Rejecting it on evidence left the original finding better supported than it was before anyone doubted it. Your turn. Take any estimate a model hands you and do not argue with the number. Ask what kind of variation it was calibrated on and whether the change you are making is that same kind. Here is a prompt to start with. The useful answer is usually the third one after it stops defending the first. The prediction was wrong. The reasoning was wronger. Working notes from a humanitarian's AI fellowship, the failures are the part worth keeping.
